  "architecture_summary": "ESalam is a .NET full-stack charity platform built on Clean Architecture with a strict inward dependency direction: Domain <- Application <- Infrastructure/Api, with Contracts acting as a shared DTO boundary. The Domain layer holds aggregate roots (Donation, Campaign, Beneficiary, ApprovalPosition) that enforce financial and workflow invariants through encapsulated state-transition methods rather than public setters. The Application layer implements a CQRS dispatch model (ICommandHandler/IQueryHandler) with thin API controllers delegating business rules downward, and defines service contracts (ICurrentUserService, IPaymentProvider, IDoubleEntryLedgerService, etc.) that Infrastructure fulfils. Money movement is guarded by two independent mechanisms: pluggable payment adapters (ToyyibPay, Chip, Stripe) behind a code-keyed factory, and a double-entry ledger with chained SHA-256 hashing for tamper-evident accounting. Two distinct front ends consume the same API: a donor-facing Blazor WebAssembly client and an operator-facing Blazor Server admin console. Persistence is PostgreSQL via Supabase, while the runtime is containerized behind an nginx TLS edge and instrumented end-to-end through an OpenTelemetry Collector fanning out to Prometheus, Tempo, Loki, and Grafana.",

### Workflow Research Report
Contains static analysis results of the codebase and business process analysis.

```json
"# System Workflow Analysis\n\n## 1. Main Workflow\n\n- **Workflow Name**: Donation Checkout and Payment Settlement Flow\n- **Description**:\n  This is the platform's core monetization path and the primary business value chain of ESalam. A donor discovers a campaign, selects a localized payment channel (Malaysian FPX online banking or card channels), and submits a donation. The API translates the request into a CQRS command, the handler resolves donor identity (authenticated user or guest session), constructs the `Donation` aggregate with its complete financial breakdown (gross amount, tip, platform fee, gateway fee, net beneficiary amount), and persists it. Payment initiation is delegated to a pluggable gateway adapter (ToyyibPay, Chip, or Stripe) resolved by provider code through `PaymentGatewayFactory`. Upon settlement, the `DoubleEntryLedgerService` writes balanced debit/credit entries with chained SHA-256 hashes, the campaign's `CollectedAmount` is incremented, and the donation is finalized (or transitioned to `Failed`/`Refunded`). A tax receipt becomes available, and the donor can review the transaction in their giving history.\n\n  This workflow is the single highest-importance path in the system (`importance: 10.0`) because it touches five domain modules simultaneously: Donor Donation, Financial Governance, Fundraising Campaign, Identity and Access, and the Platform Foundation. Any defect here propagates directly into money movement, ledger integrity, and audit compliance.\n\n- **Flow Diagram**:\n\n```mermaid\ngraph TD\n    A[Donor opens /donate/CampaignId] --> B[Donate.razor loads campaign data]\n    B --> C[Donor selects payment channel<br/>FPX bank or Card]\n    C --> D[ApiClient POSTs to api/v1/Donations]\n    D --> E[DonationsController receives request]\n    E --> F[Map to CreateDonationCommand]\n    F --> G{DonationHandlers resolves identity<br/>via ICurrentUserService}\n    G -->|Authenticated| H[Bind donor UserId]\n    G -->|Guest| I[Bind guest session context]\n    H --> J[Construct Donation aggregate<br/>amount + tip + platform fee<br/>+ gateway fee + net beneficiary]\n    I --> J\n    J --> K[Persist via IApplicationDbContext]\n    K --> L[PaymentGatewayFactory<br/>resolves adapter by code]\n    L --> M{Provider}\n    M -->|ToyyibPay| N[ToyyibPayAdapter initiates FPX session]\n    M -->|Chip| O[ChipAdapter initiates session]\n    M -->|Stripe| P[StripeAdapter initiates card session]\n    N --> Q[Return redirect URL / token to client]\n    O --> Q\n    P --> Q\n    Q --> R[Donor completes payment at gateway]\n    R --> S[Gateway callback received]\n    S --> T[Adapter verifies callback signature]\n    T --> U{Payment settled?}\n    U -->|No| V[Donation.MarkFailed]\n    U -->|Yes| W[DoubleEntryLedgerService<br/>writes balanced debit/credit entries]\n    W --> X[Compute chained SHA-256 hash<br/>over entry payload]\n    X --> Y[Campaign.CollectedAmount incremented]\n    Y --> Z[Donation finalized + receipt available]\n    Z --> AA[Donor views MyDonations history]\n    V --> AB[Failure recorded + audited]\n```\n\n- **Key Steps**:\n\n| # | Step | Component / Entry Point | Purpose |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| 1 | Campaign load and channel selection | `Donate.razor` (`/donate/{CampaignId:guid}`) | Renders campaign data, FPX bank list and card channels; resolves auth token, cart and toast services |\n| 2 | HTTP intake and command mapping | `DonationsController.cs` | Validates binding, maps the payload to `CreateDonationCommand`, normalizes result via `HandleResult` |\n| 3 | Identity resolution and aggregate construction | `DonationHandlers.cs` | Resolves donor (authenticated or guest) via `ICurrentUserService`; builds `Donation` with full money decomposition |\n| 4 | Duplicate-prevention and persistence | `IApplicationDbContext` / `Donation` aggregate | Persists via private setters and invariants; emits domain events through `BaseEntityWithEvents` |\n| 5 | Payment initiation | `PaymentAdapters.cs` → `PaymentGatewayFactory` | Resolves the provider adapter by code and initiates the provider-specific payment session |\n| 6 | Callback verification | Provider adapter (`VerifyCallbackSignature`) | Validates the inbound gateway webhook before any state mutation |\n| 7 | Settlement and ledger write | `DoubleEntryLedgerService.cs` | Records balanced debit/credit entries with chained SHA-256 hashes for tamper-evident accounting |\n| 8 | Campaign balance update | `Campaign.cs` (`CollectedAmount`) and `Donation.MarkFailed()` | Applies the terminal state transition on success or failure |\n| 9 | Receipt and history exposure | `DonationsController` → `MyDonations.razor` | Surfaces tax receipt issuance and per-donor giving history |\n\n---\n\n## 2. Other Important Workflows\n\n### 2.1 Payout Disbursement Approval Flow\n\n- **Description**:\n  The governance path that controls whether collected funds actually leave the platform. A finance officer reviews a campaign's ledger balance in the AdminWeb financial workbench and initiates a payout via `CreatePayoutCommand`, which validates available balance against `GetFinancialSummaryQuery`. The payout then traverses an ordered, cyclic, multi-step `ApprovalPosition` chain. Each reviewer action (`Approve`, `Reject`, `Escalate`, `ReturnFromEscalation`, `Skip`) is a domain state transition on `ApprovalPosition` that captures reviewer identity and free-text comments inside the domain object itself, guaranteeing a complete audit trail at the point of mutation. Step commands are authorized against the authenticated user via `ICurrentUserService`. On full approval, the ledger records the disbursement as balanced entries, permanently binding the money-out event to the same hash chain as money-in.\n\n  This workflow is critical because it enforces segregation of duties: the actor who creates a payout is not necessarily the actor who approves it, and escalation rounds create deliberate friction that a compromised single account cannot bypass.\n\n- **Flow Diagram**:\n\n```mermaid\ngraph TD\n    A[Finance officer opens<br/>PayoutsManagement.razor] --> B[Review campaign ledger balance<br/>via LedgerExplorer / summary query]\n    B --> C[Submit payout request<br/>CreatePayoutDialog]\n    C --> D[CreatePayoutCommand]\n    D --> E{Balance sufficient<br/>per ledger summary?}\n    E -->|No| F[Result.Failure returned to UI]\n    E -->|Yes| G[Payout instantiated with<br/>ordered ApprovalPosition steps]\n    G --> H[Reviewer opens<br/>PayoutApprovalStepsDialog]\n    H --> I[ApprovalDecisionDialog<br/>Approve / Reject / Skip]\n    H --> J[ApprovalEscalateDialog<br/>Escalate with rationale]\n    I --> K[ApprovePayoutStepCommand /<br/>RejectPayoutStepCommand]\n    J --> L[EscalatePayoutStepCommand]\n    K --> M[PayoutApprovalWorkflowHelper<br/>applies state transition]\n    L --> M\n    M --> N[Authorization + attribution<br/>via ICurrentUserService]\n    N --> O[Persist via IApplicationDbContext]\n    O --> P{All steps approved?}\n    P -->|Rejected| Q[Payout rejected + audited]\n    P -->|Escalated| R[New cycle created,<br/>returns to earlier step]\n    R --> H\n    P -->|Yes| S[DoubleEntryLedgerService<br/>records disbursement entries]\n    S --> T[Payout marked paid +<br/>bound to audit hash chain]\n```\n\n- **Key Steps**:\n  1. Ledger-based balance verification before any payout is created.\n  2. Payout instantiation with generated, ordered approval steps from `PositionMaster`/`PositionDefinition` templates.\n  3. Per-step decisions applied through `ApprovalPosition` state-machine methods with identity attribution and comments.\n  4. Escalation creates a new cycle rather than skipping steps — no shortcut around segregation of duties.\n  5. Terminal approval triggers an immutable ledger write for money-out.\n\n---\n\n### 2.2 Campaign Creation and Moderation Flow\n\n- **Description**:\n  A fundraiser drafts a campaign linked to a *verified* beneficiary, enriches it with story text, category taxonomy, media gallery, and capacity tiers (Qurban/Aqiqah/Waqf), then submits it into the multi-step review workflow. `CampaignHandlers` enforce ownership via `ICurrentUserService` and resolve campaigns by ID or slug. `ApprovalPositionsController` and `ApprovalPositionUseCases` generate gating steps from position templates; reviewers inspect the campaign and its media through `CampaignApprovalStepsDialog` before the campaign becomes publicly donatable. The same approval engine used for payouts is reused here, which is a deliberate architectural decision — one state machine, two governance use cases.\n\n- **Flow Diagram**:\n\n```mermaid\ngraph TD\n    A[Fundraiser opens campaign editor] --> B[Select verified beneficiary]\n    B --> C[Enter title, slug, story,<br/>target amount, category]\n    C --> D[Upload media gallery]\n    D --> E[Configure capacity tiers<br/>Qurban / Aqiqah / Waqf]\n    E --> F[POST api/v1/Campaigns<br/>CreateCampaignCommand]\n    F --> G[CampaignsController binds<br/>+ short-circuits invalid input]\n    G --> H[CampaignHandlers<br/>enforces ownership]\n    H --> I[Persist Campaign aggregate]\n    I --> J[Approval positions generated<br/>from templates in order]\n    J --> K[Reviewer inspects campaign<br/>+ media + KYC artifacts]\n    K --> L{Decision}\n    L -->|Approve| M[Advance to next step]\n    L -->|Reject| N[Return with comments to creator]\n    M --> O{All steps complete?}\n    O -->|No| K\n    O -->|Yes| P[Campaign published<br/>eligible for donations]\n    N --> A\n```\n\n---\n\n### 2.3 Identity Lifecycle and Profile Synchronization Flow\n\n- **Description**:\n  Registration, login, Supabase-linked identity binding, profile update, password change, and profile photo management. This is the primary trust boundary of the API surface because it directly handles credentials, password hashing, and identity binding. `LoginCommandHandler` supports a legacy/fallback password verification path, which is worth flagging operationally: fallback verification paths are a recurring weakness class where a downgrade in policy (weaker hash, plaintext comparison, bypassed lockout) can persist unnoticed. `RegisterCommandHandler` hashes and persists new identities through `IPasswordHasher`; `SyncProfileCommandHandler` binds a Supabase profile to the local user record. JWT issuance and validation are configured in `Program.cs`. Every other domain depends on this flow indirectly through `ICurrentUserService`.\n\n- **Flow Diagram**:\n\n```mermaid\ngraph TD\n    A[User opens /login or /register] --> B[Credentials submitted to<br/>api/v1/Auth]\n    B --> C{AuthController routes<br/>by operation}\n    C -->|Register| D[RegisterCommandHandler<br/>hash via IPasswordHasher]\n    C -->|Login| E[LoginCommandHandler]\n    C -->|Sync| F[SyncProfileCommandHandler]\n    C -->|Profile update| G[UpdateProfileCommandHandler]\n    C -->|Photo| H[Upload / DeletePhoto handlers]\n    E --> I{Credential verification}\n    I -->|Primary hash path| J[Verify via IPasswordHasher]\n    I -->|Legacy fallback path| K[Fallback verification]\n    J --> L[Issue JWT]\n    K --> L\n    D --> M[Persist UserProfile<br/>via ApplicationDbContext]\n    F --> M\n    G --> M\n    H --> N[Store media via IFileStorage]\n    L --> O[Client stores token,<br/>subsequent calls carry JWT]\n    M --> P[ICurrentUserService<br/>resolves identity downstream]\n```\n\n---\n\n### 2.4 Beneficiary Onboarding and Verification Flow\n\n- **Description**:\n  A charitable organization registers with legal identity, contact details, bank account information, and KYC media. It is persisted as a `Beneficiary` aggregate in a pending state. An operator reviews KYC artifacts in `BeneficiaryKycInspectionDialog` and invokes the domain methods `Verify`, `Reject`, or `Suspend`, which enforce encapsulation on `VerificationStatus`. Only verified beneficiaries are selectable during campaign creation — this is the KYB gate that prevents an unverified entity from being designated as a funds recipient. The banking details stored here are the destination for payout disbursements, so this flow is upstream of the payout workflow's correctness.\n\n- **Flow Diagram**:\n\n```mermaid\ngraph TD\n    A[Organization submits registration<br/>name, slug, registration no.,<br/>type, contact, bank details] --> B[BeneficiaryHandlers persists<br/>Beneficiary in pending state]\n    B --> C[Attach KYC documents<br/>BeneficiaryMedia]\n    C --> D[Operator opens<br/>BeneficiariesManagement.razor]\n    D --> E[BeneficiaryKycInspectionDialog<br/>surfaces documents]\n    E --> F{Decision}\n    F -->|Verify| G[Beneficiary.Verify]\n    F -->|Reject| H[Beneficiary.Reject]\n    G --> I[VerificationStatus = Verified]\n    H --> J[VerificationStatus = Rejected]\n    I --> K[Beneficiary selectable<br/>in campaign creation]\n    I --> L[Eligible to receive<br/>payout disbursements]\n    J --> M[Creator notified,<br/>may resubmit]\n    N[Suspend] --> O[Previously verified entity<br/>removed from eligibility]\n```\n\n---\n\n### 2.5 Transactional and Compliance Audit Flow\n\n- **Description**:\n  A cross-cutting flow that runs alongside every financially or security-relevant action. The ledger service emits audit records at the same moment it computes a chained hash, so each financial event is independently traceable in both the ledger and the audit table. `AuditTrail.razor` lets administrators search and inspect records, correlating actor, action, and timestamp. Simultaneously, OpenTelemetry instrumentation in the API, public web, and admin web emits traces, metrics, and logs to the `otel-collector`, which fans out metrics to Prometheus (namespace `esalam`, exporter on 8889), spans to Tempo, and logs to Loki, all surfaced in provisioned Grafana dashboards. Prometheus scrapes every 5 seconds — aggressive enough for near-real-time operational visibility.\n\n- **Flow Diagram**:\n\n```mermaid\ngraph TD\n    A[Financial or security-relevant action] --> B[Ledger write / handler execution]\n    B --> C[DoubleEntryLedgerService<br/>computes chained SHA-256]\n    C --> D[IAuditService emits<br/>audit record]\n    D --> E[(Audit table)]\n    B --> F[OpenTelemetry instrumentation<br/>emits span + metrics + logs]\n    F --> G[OTLP receiver<br/>gRPC 4317 / HTTP 4318]\n    G --> H[batch + memory_limiter<br/>processors]\n    H --> I[Export fan-out]\n    I --> J[Prometheus exporter 8889<br/>namespace: esalam]\n    I --> K[Tempo OTLP/gRPC]\n    I --> L[Loki push API]\n    J --> M[Prometheus scrape<br/>every 5s]\n    E --> N[AuditTrail.razor]\n    N --> O[AuditInspectionDialog]\n    M --> P[Grafana dashboards]\n    K --> P\n    L --> P\n```\n\n---\n\n## 3. Workflow Insights\n\n### 3.1 Structural Observations\n\n- **Single approval engine, two governance paths.** Campaign moderation and payout disbursement both drive the same `ApprovalPosition` state machine with the same five transitions (`Approve`, `Reject`, `Escalate`, `ReturnFromEscalation`, `Skip`). This is a strong design choice: less code to audit, identical audit semantics, and certification/review effort spent once. It also means a single defect in the state machine compromises *both* governance boundaries simultaneously — the blast radius is doubled.\n- **Money movement is architecturally separated from donor intent.** The `Donation` aggregate holds the money decomposition but never initiates payment itself; payment initiation and settlement live in `PaymentAdapters` and `DoubleEntryLedgerService` respectively. This separation means a compromised donation-creation endpoint does not automatically grant payment-initiation primitive access — a meaningful containment property.\n- **Tamper-evidence is chained, not merely append-only.** The SHA-256 chain over entry payloads means retroactive modification of any historical ledger entry breaks verification at every subsequent entry. This is the strongest auditability property in the system and the reason `DoubleEntryLedgerService` is rated `importance: 0.96`.\n- **Dual identity model adds state complexity.** The cart and donation validation paths serve both guests (localStorage-backed) and authenticated donors. `CartController` is explicitly the most stateful controller in the system because it bridges two identity models with dual persistence. Merge semantics between guest state and authenticated state is a high-risk correctness boundary.\n- **The trust boundary is credential-adjacent and quiet.** `AuthHandlers.cs` is rated the highest-risk file in its directory because it contains `LoginCommandHandler` with a *legacy/fallback* password verification path. Fallback paths are a classic downgrade vector: if the primary path enforces modern hashing and the fallback path does not, an attacker who can force the fallback (e.g., by manipulating lookup keys or profile linkage) bypasses the strong check entirely.\n\n### 3.2 Optimization Opportunities\n\n| Area | Observation | Opportunity |\n|---|---|---|\n| Payment adapter duplication | ToyyibPay, Chip, and Stripe adapters each implement initiation and signature verification independently | Extract a shared `PaymentIntent` normalization layer so callback verification logic is written once and reused; reduce per-provider audit scope |\n| Approval workflow reuse | Same state machine reused correctly | Expose it as a formal, tested library boundary with contract tests, so new governed entities (e.g., refund approval) inherit verified behavior |\n| Campaign balance update | `CollectedAmount` and donation finalization appear as sequential steps after settlement | Wrap in an explicit transaction with optimistic concurrency on `Campaign` to prevent lost updates under concurrent donations to the same campaign |\n| Telemetry granularity | 5-second Prometheus scrape is aggressive across all services | Consider splitting high-value financial metrics (ledger write latency, settlement success rate) onto a tighter scrape than generic HTTP metrics |\n| Auth fallback path | Legacy verification path coexists with primary path | Instrument which path is taken per login; if fallback usage is non-zero and unexplained, investigate. Ideally migrate and retire |\n| Guest-to-auth cart merge | Dual persistence requires explicit merge | Make merge an explicit idempotent operation with a documented conflict policy, and test concurrent cart modifications during login |\n\n### 3.3 Workflow Dependencies\n\n- **Donation Checkout** depends on **Campaign** (must be published and beneficiary-verified), **Identity** (reliable identity resolution or explicit guest context), and **Financial Governance** (payment initiation and ledger settlement). A failure in beneficiary verification propagates upward as a campaign that should not be donatable still accepting donations.\n- **Payout Disbursement** depends on **Financial Read Models** (ledger-derived balance) and **Approval Workflow** (authorized step decisions) and, transitively, on the **cryptographic integrity of the ledger itself**. If the ledger balance can be manipulated, balance validation is meaningless.\n- **Campaign Creation and Moderation** is the *sole* entry point into the donatable campaign population. Any bypass of the approval gate directly injects unreviewed campaigns into the donation checkout path.\n- **Audit and Observability** is not a leaf dependency — it is a parallel obligation on every financial write. If `IAuditService` emission is not transactionally coupled to the ledger write, a crash between the two produces an unaudited money movement. This coupling should be verified explicitly.\n- **Beneficiary Verification** gates campaign creation, which gates donations, which gates payouts. It is the deepest upstream dependency in the money chain and the cheapest place to inject an illegitimate funds recipient.\n\n### 3.4 Validation Against Documented Business Processes\n\nThe research materials describe the business intent as: *\"a donor discovers a campaign, selects a localized payment channel, completes a donation; funds are recorded in an immutable double-entry ledger with chained cryptographic hashes; operators and beneficiaries are onboarded through KYB-style verification; disbursement is gated behind multi-step, role-attributed approval; the value proposition is trust — separation of donor intent from money movement.\"*\n\n**Consistent findings:**\n- The five documented workflows map cleanly onto the domain module inventory; no step in the documented business process lacks a code entry point.\n- Segregation of duties is genuinely enforced at the domain layer — `ApprovalPosition` transitions capture reviewer identity and comments as first-class domain state, not as a peripheral log.\n- Payment vendor abstraction (`IPaymentProvider` + code-keyed factory) matches the documented de-risking-of-vendor-lock-in claim.\n\n**Discrepancies and gaps worth flagging:**\n\n1. **Ledger-audit transactional coupling is asserted but not evidenced.** The materials state audit records are emitted \"alongside\" hash computation, but the workflow as described does not confirm whether this is a single transaction. Documented compliance claim ⇒ needs explicit verification.\n2. **Refund path is modeled but not documented as a workflow.** `Donation.cs` exposes `Refund`, but no workflow in the materials describes the refund lifecycle, its approval requirements, or how a refund entry is written back into the chained ledger. This is a gap between domain capability and documented process.\n3. **Recurring donations and reservations lack a documented governance path.** Both are listed as sub-modules (`RecurringHandlers`, `ReservationHandlers`) with use cases for schedules and capacity release, but no business flow describes how a recurring charge settles through the ledger or who authorizes capacity revocation.\n4. **Legacy password fallback is undocumented.** The fallback verification path in `LoginCommandHandler` appears in code but not in the described identity flow. Any authentication downgrade path should be a documented, monitored decision rather than an implicit branch.\n5. **Guest donation attribution.** The materials note guest donations are permitted, but no workflow step describes how a guest donation is later attributed (or deliberately never attributed) to an account, and how that interacts with tax receipt issuance and anonymity flags — both of which require a fundable identity.\n6. **`SimulatePayment` is a production-reachable test primitive.** `DonationHandlers` includes a simulate-payment capability. If this endpoint is reachable in the production API surface without strict authorization, it permits donation finalization and ledger entry creation without any real gateway settlement — a direct integrity bypass of the entire primary workflow. This must be explicitly gated by environment and role.\n\n---\n\n*Document generated from source code insights and domain research. Enforcement verdicts marked as assertions requiring verification are intentionally left as gaps rather than assumed correct.*"
```

      "purpose": "other",
      "subdirectory_count": 0,
      "summary": "The `compose` directory is the deployment/orchestration configuration layer for the eSalam platform, containing four Docker Compose manifests that define how the ASP.NET Core API (`esalam-api`), public/admin web frontends, reverse proxy, and the full observability stack (OTel Collector, Tempo, Loki, Prometheus) are built, networked, and run across local, production, and observability environments. The manifests are layered by concern: `docker-compose.yml` is the default runtime definition (prebuilt GHCR image + env-injected secrets), `docker-compose.prod.yml` adds the nginx TLS reverse proxy and real frontends, `docker-compose.observability.yml` isolates telemetry collectors, and `docker-compose copy.yml` is a stray duplicate that leaks a plaintext Supabase Postgres connection string. Together they form the single source of truth for environment topology, port exposure, service dependencies, and secret wiring for the backend — but they carry no business logic themselves."

      "summary": "This directory contains multiple file groups. Key aspects: SCSS theme partials for the Radzen Blazor component library — one file per UI component (accordion, grid, dialog, datepicker, etc.). Each file declares Sass variables with !default (allowing theme overrides) whose values point at CSS custom properties (--rz-*), followed by the component's class rules. This batch covers components A–P; it is pure presentation layer with no business logic, data access, or API surface. This batch of the blazor stylesheet directory contains the second half of Radzen Blazor's component theme layer — per-component SCSS partials for advanced widgets (Scheduler, Pivot DataGrid, Sankey, Spider chart, Tabs, Tree, Timeline, Upload, SpeechToText) plus foundational layout/utility partials (_utilities, _typography, _spacing, _stack, _sidebar). Every file follows the same pattern: declare overridable SCSS variables with `!default` bound to CSS custom properties (`var(--rz-*)`), then emit `.rz-*` class rules, BEM modifiers, and size/state variants. Together they form the presentation contract for the component library — no business logic, but they define the theming API surface consumed by every Radzen component and any downstream app theme."

      "summary": "The Campaigns directory is the core domain-entity package for the CharityPlatform campaign bounded context, housing the aggregate roots and supporting entities that model fundraising campaigns, their categories, and the multi-step approval workflow positions required before payouts. Campaign.cs defines the Campaign aggregate plus its Category lookup entity, while PositionMaster.cs, PositionDefinition.cs and ApprovalPosition.cs form the configurable approval-hierarchy subsystem that determines which positions (and which users/roles) must sign off on a campaign or payout based on target amount. All types inherit BaseEntity, use private setters with behavior methods (Approve/Reject/Escalate/Skip, SetActive) and consume shared Enums, ValueObjects and Identity/Beneficiaries/Financial entities, marking this as a rich persistence-oriented domain layer rather than thin DTOs."

      "summary": "This directory contains multiple file groups. Key aspects: The Pages directory contains the Blazor routable page components for the ESalam e-commerce/campaign application, each declared with an @page directive and rendered by the client-side router. The files collectively implement storefront navigation: informational pages (About, Contact), campaign catalog and detail views, and the shopping cart, all sharing common patterns such as breadcrumbs, @inject service dependencies, Localization via Lang, and IDisposable for cleanup. This is a frontend presentation layer that orchestrates injected backend services (ApiClient, CartService, ToastService, LocalStorageService) rather than containing business logic itself. This directory contains the Blazor (Razor) front-end page components that form the primary user-facing surface of the ESalam donation platform, covering the home landing page, campaign donation flow, donation receipt/status, donor login, donation history, NGO/beneficiary profiles, FAQ, and global error handling. Each .razor file combines an @page route directive, dependency-injected services (ApiClient, AuthService, ToastService, CartService, LocalStorageService, IJSRuntime, LanguageService), and inline styling/markup to render a complete routed screen. The pages collectively gate authentication-aware flows (donation, history) and consume the backend API layer through the injected ApiClient, making them the main integration points between UI and business logic. This batch contains Blazor Razor page components for the ESalam charity platform, covering the simulated payment gateway, donor profile/settings, Qurban sacrifice campaigns, registration, password reset, tax exemption info, and ledger verification. Each .razor file is a routable page using @page directives, dependency-injected services (ApiClient, AuthService, LanguageService, ToastService, LocalStorageService) and shared responsive layout containers, collectively forming the donor-facing UI surface. The lone .razor.css file is an empty stub documenting that styles were merged into the global wwwroot/app.css."
